units.title: The Subject Matter of Geography
units.intro: Geography studies the Earth as the home of people — **where** things are and **why** they are there. Two big halves: **physical** (land, weather, water, living cover) and **human** (population, settlements, economy). Modern fields: geomorphology, climatology, biogeography, economic, population, political, cartography. The glue is **spatial** thinking: location, place, region, movement, human–environment.

cards.title: 1.1 Understanding Geography
body: Sub-unit 1.1 presents the definition of geography and discusses its importance in providing basic knowledge about the world.
The sub-unit also presents the history of geography in brief.
Geography is the study of the earth and its lands, features, inhabitants and phenomena.

The word geography comes from a Greek word that means “earth description.” Studying how things are organized on the earth provides useful information to understand environmental changes caused by people.
Problems related to food supply, the environment or development can also be easily understood through geographic knowledge and skills.

cards.title: 1.2 Fields of Modern Geography
body: Modern geography is unique as it studies the world from at different points including both man-made and natural features of the earth’s surface.

For example, a geographer who studies the growing of wheat in a particular region needs information on the climate, soil and landform of the region as well as knowledge about the transport network and the price of wheat.
Geographers today not only describe things, but they also attempt to explain why things are distributed over the earth as they are.
Human Geography: Human geography is the study of the relationships between human beings and the natural environment.
Human geography covers a number of fields.

units.title: The Earth-Sun Relation
units.intro:
Earth is a planet in the solar system, slightly flattened ball. **Rotation** (spin on its axis, ~24 h) → day and night, apparent daily path of the Sun, Coriolis deflection of winds (preview). Axis tilt ~23½°.

**Revolution** (orbit ~365¼ days) + tilt → seasons: when the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun it is northern summer (June solstice, Tropic of Cancer 23½°N gets overhead sun). December opposite. Equinoxes: equal day and night, sun over equator.

cards.title: 2.1 Introducing the Universe
body: The universe consists of many types of planets, moons, countless stars, comets, meteors, meteorites, and asteroids.

body: The plane in which the earth‘s orbit is known as the plane of ecliptic.

cards.q: What is the speed of Earth's rotation at the North and South Poles?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze how rotational speed varies with latitude.**
Rotational speed is proportional to the circumference of latitude. Circumference decreases poleward.

**Step 2: Evaluate at the poles.**
At the geographic poles, the latitude circle shrinks to a single point. Its circumference is zero.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the speed of rotation at the poles is **0 km/h**.

tips.text: The spinning of the earth on its own axis from west to east is called rotation.
The earth takes about 24 hours to complete a rotation.
The axial plane of the earth is inclined to the plane of the earth’s orbit at an angle of 66 ½0.
The different kinds of weather that occur over land and bodies of water are the results of the earth’s rotation on its own axis.
The length of day andnight and the apparent movement of the sun are also caused by the earth’s rotation and the angle of its orbital plane as well.
The movement of the earth around the sun is called a revolution.
The earth takes one year or 365 ¼ days to complete one orbit around the sun.
The extra hours are added to make one full day every four years or a leap year.
Due to the elliptical shape of the earth’s orbit the sun appears closer (perihelion) and further (aphelion) from the earth at different seasons of the year.
The revolution of the earth causes the variation of the length of days and nights and, seasons of the year.

units.title: Weather and Climate
units.intro:
Atmosphere layers (troposphere = weather kitchen). Weather = short-term state. Climate = long-term average. Elements: temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, clouds, precipitation.

Temperature: latitude, altitude (~6.5 °C / 1000 m), land/sea, clouds, ocean currents. Pressure: high = sinking dry; low = rising rain. Wind blows from high to low pressure; named from where it comes. Belts: trades, westerlies, polar. ITCZ = meeting of trades, rain. Precipitation: rain, snow, hail — convectional, orographic, frontal.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Nitrogen and Oxygen together account for approximately what percentage of the total volume of the atmosphere?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the gas concentrations in the atmosphere.**
- Nitrogen ($N_2$): $78\%$
- Oxygen ($O_2$): $21\%$

**Step 2: Sum the percentages.**
$$\text{Total} = 78\% + 21\% = 99\%$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
Together they account for **99%** of the atmospheric volume.

- Climatology: long-term weather averages over decades ($30+\text{ years}$).

**Step 2: Match with the scientist's title.**
A scientist specializing in climatology is a Climatologist.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct term is **Climatologist**.

tips.text: In geography, when we speak about temperature we usually mean the hotness or coldness of the air around us. This heat is received by the atmosphere in different ways.

The atmosphere of the earth extends upwards for several thousand kilometers. It is composed of different gases, dusts, moistures, smoke particles etc.
This force of pressing of gases and others from the top of the atmosphere down to the ground is called air pressure.
Air pressure is influenced by altitude and temperature the density of air decreases upwards with altitude.

units.title: Concept of Region
units.intro: A **region** is an area with one or more shared features that make it different from neighbours. Formal (uniform) region: same climate or language. Functional: organised around a node (a city and its hinterland). Vernacular: a name people use (“the highlands”). Regions nest: a farm inside a district inside a country. Boundaries can be sharp (a coast) or fuzzy (a language mix).

cards.title: 4.1 Place Similarity and Regions
body: For many years, geographers debated whether regions exist naturally, or they are simply created by people.

A region defined on the basis of two or more features is called a multiple-feature region.
For example, a soil region is a single-feature physical region while a climate region is a multiple-feature physical region.

Regions are identified and delimited using similarities.
Only one criterion or feature may be used to define single-feature regions, while the use of two or more criteria defines multiple-feature regions.
When the criteria used are physical features, we have natural regions; when we use cultural features, we have cultural regions.

units.title: Landforms
units.intro:
Landform = shape of the land. Continental crust is thicker and less dense than oceanic. Large forms: mountains, plateaus, plains, valleys, rift. Built by internal energy (uplift, volcano, fault — preview of Grade 11 plates) and carved by external (weathering, rivers, wind, ice, waves).

Ocean floor: continental shelf, slope, rise, abyssal plain, ridge, trench, island arc. Eritrea sits by a young rift / Red Sea — a living classroom for “the crust can split.”

body: Hills are small landforms, about 600 meters from their adjacent area.
A valley is a low-lying land bounded by higher ground.
A plateau is a highland with steep slopes, and is a broad and fairly flat top.
If the plateau is bounded on one side by a mountain or a ridge and on the other side by a steep slope it is called Piedmont plateau.
The Deccan plateau of India is a good example.

tips.text: The surface of the earth is not uniform. These ups and downs are called landforms.
Landforms are the natural features of the landscape.
Landforms are different in shape and height. There are different landforms on continental crust.
The main landforms on the continental crust are plains, valleys, hills, plateaus, and mountains. Each landform has its own characteristics that distinguish it from others which are noticeable.

Plains are broad, flat areas of altitude. Their altitudes are reaching up to 150 meters above sea level. There are different kinds of plains based on the origin of formation such as coastal plain and destructional plain.
Hills are small landforms little higher than their surrounding areas while valleys are low-lying land bounded by higher ground.
Rivers and streams flow through valleys.
Plateaus are highlands with steep slopes and a broad and fairly flat top. There are different kinds of plateaus that differ in their shape and formation.
Mountains are highlands with the highest elevation. Their altitude is greater than 1000 meters above their bases.
Most mountains are found fairly close together.
